lead: This unit shows how gears are chosen, sized and arranged into a gearbox that survives its service life. You start from the law of gearing, move through materials and the design of spur, helical, bevel and worm gears, then use gear trains and ray diagrams to build multi-speed boxes. After it you can size a gear pair for bending, wear and life, and lay out the stages of a gearbox.
about: The unit builds in one line: geometry, material, stress, life, arrangement. Chapter 7.1 fixes the names and the law of gearing that every later formula assumes. Chapter 7.2 chooses the material and heat treatment that set the allowable stresses. Chapters 7.3 to 7.6 apply those allowables to spur, helical, straight bevel and worm gears, adding the extra loads each type brings: dynamic load, axial thrust, cone geometry and sliding wear. Chapter 7.7 changes the view from one pair to a train of pairs, including the epicyclic train. Chapter 7.8 adds life and the rest of the gearbox: bearings, heat and lubrication. Chapter 7.9 arranges several gear pairs into a multi-speed box and reads the result on a ray diagram.

chapters.idea: A gear pair transmits motion at a constant ratio only if the common normal at every contact point passes through the pitch point; the involute profile does this.
chapters.depth: Spur, helical, bevel, worm and rack and pinion; internal and external gears. Nomenclature: pitch circle diameter d, number of teeth z, module m = d/z in mm, circular pitch p = πm, diametral pitch in inches, addendum, dedendum, clearance, working depth, pressure angle φ (20° standard), base circle diameter d cosφ, contact ratio. Law of gearing and why involute satisfies it; interference and undercutting in brief. Some syllabi call the module the metric module and the diametral pitch the English module.

figure.aria: A tree groups gears into spur, helical, bevel, worm and rack types by shaft arrangement.

chapters.example: A 20° involute spur pair has z1 = 20, z2 = 60 and module 4 mm. Find both pitch diameters, the centre distance, both base circle diameters and the velocity ratio. Answers: d1 = 80 mm, d2 = 240 mm, a = 160 mm, db1 = 75.2 mm, db2 = 225.5 mm, ratio 3.
chapters.trap: Mixing module with circular pitch, and using the addendum or base circle instead of the pitch circle when applying m = d/z. The law of gearing is about the common normal, not the common tangent.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for fits and tolerances; school geometry of circles and triangles.
chapters.leave: Tooth stress to Chapter 7.3; trains to Chapter 7.7; manufacturing to a production course.

chapters.idea: Gear material is a system of core strength, surface hardness and heat treatment, chosen to match load, speed and cost.
chapters.depth: Cast irons, plain carbon steels (0.3-0.6% C), alloy steels with Cr, Ni and Mo, case-carburising, through-hardening, nitriding and induction hardening; non-metals: nylon, bakelite and bronze for worm wheels. Properties: bending strength, surface hardness in BHN, wear resistance, machinability, distortion in heat treatment. Pinion is made harder than the gear by about 30-50 BHN to balance life. Selection by peripheral speed, shock, size and availability. Some syllabi list only cast iron, steel and bronze; a few universities add sintered and plastic gears.

figure.aria: A flow chart takes load and speed to a material family, heat treatment, surface hardness and a strength check.

chapters.example: A 7.5 kW motor at 1440 rpm drives a 20-tooth pinion of module 3 mm with moderate shock. Find the pitch line velocity and recommend a material pair. d = 60 mm, v = π(0.060)(1440)/60 = 4.52 m/s. Below about 5 m/s, a through-hardened C45 pinion at 250 BHN running with a cast iron gear is a common shop-floor choice; above it, use a case-carburised alloy steel pinion.
chapters.trap: Choosing the hardest steel for both wheels. The pinion has more cycles, so it must be harder; and a hard surface needs a tough core. Hardness in BHN is not strength in MPa.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 material properties; Chapter 7.1 for module and pitch diameter.
chapters.leave: Heat-treatment furnace practice to manufacturing; allowable stress numbers to Chapter 7.3.

chapters.idea: A spur tooth is a cantilever, so Lewis sizes it for bending and Buckingham adds the dynamic and wear loads that a static formula misses.
chapters.depth: Lewis equation Ft = σb b m y (or σb b πm Y with Y = πy), Lewis form factor y from tooth count and pressure angle, face width b = 8m to 12m, velocity factor Cv, Buckingham dynamic load Fd with deformation factor C and pitch line velocity in m/s, wear load Fw = d1 b Q K, Q = 2z2/(z1+z2), load-stress factor K, design checks Fd ≤ Fw and Ft ≤ beam strength. Standard 20° full-depth involute. Some syllabi call the Buckingham load the dynamic load and the wear load the limiting load for wear.

figure.aria: A flow chart runs from tooth and module choice through Lewis strength, Buckingham dynamic load and wear check to a safe or revised design.

chapters.example: A 20° spur pinion with 20 teeth, allowable bending stress 120 MPa and face width 10m transmits 10 kW at 1200 rpm. Take Lewis form factor y = 0.32 and find the module by Lewis. Pitch diameter d = 20m mm, so v = π(0.020m)(1200)/60 = 1.257m m/s with m in mm. Ft = 10000/(1.257m) = 7958/m N. Beam strength = 120(10m)(m)(0.32) = 384m² N. Equating gives m³ = 20.7, so m = 2.75 mm; choose standard m = 3 mm.
chapters.trap: Using the Lewis strength as if it were the applied load, and forgetting the velocity factor when power is converted to tangential force. Face width in mm and module in mm must match; do not mix with metres.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 7.1 and 7.2; Units 1 and 2 for bending stress and fatigue.
chapters.leave: Helical and bevel factors to Chapters 7.4 and 7.5; bearing reactions to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Helical teeth share load over a longer contact line, so they carry more load quietly but produce an axial thrust that changes bearing and shaft design.
chapters.depth: Helix angle ψ, normal module mn, transverse module mt = mn/cosψ, normal pressure angle φn and transverse φt with tanφn = tanφt cosψ, virtual teeth zv = z/cos³ψ, modified Lewis with mn and y for zv, velocity factor, axial thrust Fa = Ft tanψ, radial force, overlap and contact ratio, hand of helix. Some syllabi use β for helix angle and call zv the formative number of teeth. Double helical and herringbone in one line.

figure.aria: A chain shows tangential load creating axial thrust, which becomes a bearing thrust load and drives bearing choice.

chapters.example: A helical pair has mn = 3 mm, z1 = 20, z2 = 80, ψ = 15°, b = 45 mm, and transmits 11 kW at 1450 rpm. Find mt, d1, v, Ft, Fa and zv1. mt = 3/cos15° = 3.106 mm, d1 = 62.1 mm, v = π(0.0621)(1450)/60 = 4.71 m/s, Ft = 11000/4.71 = 2335 N, Fa = 2335 tan15° = 626 N, zv1 = 20/cos³15° = 22.2.
chapters.trap: Putting the transverse module into a Lewis equation written for the normal module, and leaving the axial thrust out of the shaft and bearing loads. Convert the helix angle to radians only inside a calculator that needs it.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.3 for Lewis; Chapter 7.1 for profiles.
chapters.leave: Thrust bearing selection to Unit 5; gearbox heat and lubrication to Chapter 7.8.

chapters.idea: Bevel gears turn the drive through an angle, and their teeth are designed as a virtual spur gear on the back cone, using the mean cone distance for load.
chapters.depth: Straight bevel nomenclature: pitch cone angle γ, cone distance R, face width b, addendum and dedendum at the back cone, crown. For a 90° shaft angle tanγ1 = z1/z2 and γ2 = 90° - γ1; R = d1/(2 sinγ1); b ≤ R/3; virtual teeth zv = z/cosγ; mean radius rm = R - b/2 and mean module mm = m rm/R; modified Lewis at the mean section; Buckingham dynamic load; thrust loads from the tangential force. Spiral bevel and hypoid in one line only.

figure.aria: A tree lists the pinion cone angle, gear cone angle, cone distance and virtual teeth of a 90 degree bevel pair.

chapters.example: A 90° straight bevel pair has z1 = 20, z2 = 40, module 4 mm at the large end and face width 30 mm. Find d1, d2, γ1, γ2, R, mean cone distance and mean module. d1 = 80 mm, d2 = 160 mm, γ1 = tan⁻¹(20/40) = 26.57°, γ2 = 63.43°, R = √(40² + 80²) = 89.44 mm, Rm = 89.44 - 15 = 74.44 mm, mm = 4(74.44/89.44) = 3.33 mm.
chapters.trap: Using the actual tooth count in the Lewis form factor instead of zv, and taking the tangential load at the outer radius instead of the mean radius. Cone angles add to the shaft angle, not to 180°.
chapters.leave: Spiral bevel design to an advanced course; bearing loads to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A worm drive gives a large reduction in one step through sliding contact, so wear, friction and heat set the size more than bending strength.
chapters.depth: Worm with one to four starts zw, worm wheel z2, lead L = zw px, lead angle λ with tanλ = L/(πd1), module m, diametral quotient q with d1 = qm, d2 = mz2, ratio i = z2/zw, sliding velocity vs = v1/cosλ, friction angle φ and efficiency η = tanλ/tan(λ+φ), self-locking when λ < φ, worm wheel in phosphor bronze, worm in hardened and ground steel, Lewis strength check on the wheel, wear check and heat check. Some syllabi call q the diametral quotient or the worm factor.

figure.aria: Efficiency curves rise with lead angle and flatten, with the higher friction curve lying lower.

chapters.example: A single-start worm has z1 = 1, z2 = 40, module 5 mm, q = 10 and runs at 1440 rpm. Find d1, d2, lead, lead angle and sliding velocity. d1 = qm = 50 mm, d2 = mz2 = 200 mm, lead = πm = 15.7 mm, tanλ = 15.7/(π×50) = 0.1 so λ = 5.71°, v1 = π(0.050)(1440)/60 = 3.77 m/s, vs = 3.77/cos5.71° = 3.79 m/s.
chapters.trap: Using d1 = m z1 for the worm, which is wrong; the worm diameter is set by q. Also reversing the ratio, and forgetting that the efficiency formula uses the friction angle, not the pressure angle.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 7.1 and 7.2; Unit 5 for lubrication and friction.
chapters.leave: Detailed thermal rating to Chapter 7.8; bearing selection to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A gear train multiplies ratios along its pairs, and an epicyclic train is solved by adding the carrier rotation to the relative rotations of the gears.
chapters.depth: Simple, compound and reverted trains; train value = product of driven teeth / product of driver teeth; sign for direction. Epicyclic: sun, planet, ring and carrier; tabulation method; relative angular speeds; Willis equation; torque balance on the carrier; applications in the differential, lathe back gear and planetary hub. Some syllabi call the epicyclic train a planetary gear train.

figure.aria: A graph shows a sun meshing with a planet, the planet meshing with a ring, and a carrier pinned to the planet.

chapters.example: An epicyclic train has sun z = 24, planet z = 18 and ring z = 60. The sun is fixed and the carrier turns at 100 rpm clockwise. Find the ring speed and direction. Tabulation gives ring = -1.4 × carrier, so the ring turns at 140 rpm anticlockwise.
chapters.trap: Treating an epicyclic train as a simple ratio z_driven/z_driver. The speeds must be measured relative to the carrier first; adding absolute speeds gives the wrong direction and magnitude.
chapters.leave: Multi-speed selection to Chapter 7.9; tooth stresses to Chapter 7.3.

chapters.idea: Gears accumulate damage over their load history, so a gearbox is sized by an equivalent life load and then checked for bearings, heat and lubrication.
chapters.depth: Gear life in cycles, S-N curve for bending and contact, endurance limit, Miner rule and equivalent load with exponent 3 for contact, service factor, design life in hours, single and multistage gearbox layout, ratio split, housing, oil level, splash and forced lubrication, heat balance, seals. Some syllabi call the equivalent load the cubic mean load. Reliability in one line.

figure.aria: A flow chart moves from load spectrum to equivalent load, gear size, shafts and bearings, heat and lubrication, and housing.

chapters.example: A gearbox runs at 1000 rpm for 10,000 h with 10 kW for 60% of the time, 6 kW for 30% and 2 kW for 10%. Find the equivalent power for a life exponent of 3. Peq = (0.6×10³ + 0.3×6³ + 0.1×2³)^(1/3) = (600 + 64.8 + 0.8)^(1/3) = 8.73 kW. Total cycles = 1000×60×10000 = 6×10^8 cycles.
chapters.trap: Using the maximum load for the whole life or the simple average load. Life is counted in cycles, not hours; and a gearbox can fail first on heat or bearing life, not tooth bending.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 7.3-7.6; Unit 2 fatigue; Unit 5 bearings and lubrication.
chapters.leave: Bearing life formula to Unit 5; detailed housing drawing to design practice.

chapters.idea: A multi-speed gearbox is a product of gear groups, and a ray diagram shows the resulting spindle speeds on a log scale so the steps and overlaps are visible.
chapters.depth: Speed range Rn = nmax/nmin, number of steps z, geometric progression with step ratio φ = (Rn)^(1/(z-1)), standard φ values, arithmetic versus geometric, ray diagram (speed chart) with shaft lines and rays, structure formula, grouping, ratio limits 1/4 to 4, gearing diagram, sliding gear and Norton drives. Some syllabi call the ray diagram the speed diagram. Only a few universities teach structure formulae in detail.

figure.aria: A chain shows an input speed passing through a two-ratio group and a three-ratio group to give six speeds.

chapters.example: A 6-speed gearbox has minimum speed 100 rpm and step ratio φ = 1.41. Find the six spindle speeds. n1 = 100, n2 = 141, n3 = 199, n4 = 280, n5 = 395, n6 = 557 rpm approximately. The maximum is 557 rpm and the range is 5.57.
chapters.trap: Using an arithmetic progression because the numbers look neat; gearbox speeds are geometric. On a ray diagram, rays that cross or speeds that overlap mean the layout is wrong.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.7 for train ratios; Chapter 7.8 for gearbox layout.
chapters.leave: Automatic and hydrostatic transmissions to advanced courses; detailed ray-diagram construction methods to design handbooks.
